title: Moosewala Returns to a Toronto Stage as a Hologram as Toddler Brother Recreates His Thaapi
excerpt: The 'Signed to God' hologram tour opened to a packed Scotiabank Arena, where two-year-old Shubhdeep's thaapi became the night's defining moment. US dates follow in New York, Houston and Oakland.
body:
• Sidhu Moosewala's "Signed to God" hologram world tour opened to a packed Scotiabank Arena in Toronto on October 9, with a 3D projection of the singer performing to his original vocals.
  • The night's most shared moment: his two-year-old brother Shubhdeep, known as Chhota Sidhu, recreated Moosewala's signature thaapi thigh-slap on stage alongside their parents.
  • Moosewala's song "295" is nearing 900 million views on YouTube; 17 songs have been released since his 2022 murder, with more to come, his father told the crowd.
  • The tour continues to Vancouver and Calgary in Canada, then New York, Houston and Oakland in the US.

Four years after his murder, Sidhu Moosewala performed in Toronto again — as light. The opening night of the "Signed to God" hologram world tour filled the Scotiabank Arena on October 9, projecting a 3D recreation of the Punjabi singer onto the stage to perform to his original vocals, in what organisers billed as a first-of-its-kind show for an Indian artist.

The performance centred on "295," the song that became an anthem after his death and is now approaching 900 million views and 12 million likes on his YouTube channel. But the moment that travelled furthest on social media belonged to the smallest person on stage.

Chhota Sidhu's thaapi

Moosewala's parents, Balkaur Singh and Charan Kaur, attended the opening with their younger son Shubhdeep, born in March 2024 and known to fans as Chhota Sidhu. On stage, the two-year-old recreated his brother's signature thaapi — the thigh-slap gesture that was a fixture of Moosewala's performances — drawing an eruption from the crowd and a wave of phone footage that spread across Punjabi social media within hours. "It's as if Sidhu Moose Wala were still alive among us," one fan posted on X.

https://x.com/abplive/status/2109125566960214019

"To get justice, we need power, for which I am again fighting."

— Balkaur Singh, Moosewala's father, addressing the Toronto crowd

A celebration shadowed by an unsolved grief

Balkaur Singh used the evening to return to the family's central demand. Moosewala was shot dead in Punjab's Mansa district in 2022; police have alleged that people linked to the Bishnoi gang, including Canada-based gangster Goldy Brar, were involved in the killing. His father told the Toronto audience the family has been seeking justice for over four years, and that efforts to silence the singer had failed: 17 songs have been released since his death, with another set on the way.

What the tour means for the diaspora

Toronto was a deliberate first stop. Canada's Punjabi diaspora was Moosewala's second home market — he lived and recorded in Brampton before returning to Punjab — and the arena-scale turnout shows his audience has grown, not faded, since 2022. The hologram format raises obvious questions about artistry and consent that the music industry is only beginning to answer, but for the fans in the arena the transaction was simpler: a night with a voice many believed they would never hear in a room again. The tour now moves to Vancouver and Calgary, then crosses to the United States for New York, Houston and Oakland — the shows US-based fans can still plan for. Reporting by NDTV and Mint.
